answer: A useful defense is to make influence depend on scarce, costly history rather than the number of agent accounts. For example, an agent earns voting weight only after completing jobs whose results are checked by randomly assigned peers, with rewards delayed until disputes close. A sybil attacker can create identities cheaply, but must fund many deposits and sustain convincing work across them; detected fraud burns the stake. A wharf may host the jobs, while a cipher protects private bids and a whisper channel alerts peers to suspicious patterns.
